title: Out of a hundred
objectives: Read a percentage as a count of hundredths
Move between fractions, decimals and percentages

screens.title: Out of a hundred
screens.prose: Fees, interest rates and fund returns are all quoted as percentages. We will see what a percentage counts, and give it two other names.
This square is cut into 100 equal cells. Some of them are shaded.
screens.question: What fraction of the whole square is shaded? Give a fraction or a decimal.

hints.text: Count the full rows first, then the extra cells.
The fourth row is only partly shaded. Each full row above it holds 10 cells.
Three full rows is 30 cells, and 7 more makes 37. That is 37 out of 100.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the shaded cells, then compare with all 100.

byKey.count: You gave the number of shaded cells. The question asks what part of the whole that is: 37 cells out of 100.
byKey.thousandths: You wrote 37 thousandths. Each cell is one hundredth of the square, so 37 cells is 37 hundredths.
byKey.rows: You counted the three full rows and left out the 7 cells in the fourth row.

explain.text: You counted 37 cells out of 100, so the shaded part is $\tfrac{37}{100} = 0.37$ of the square. Each cell is one hundredth. Counting in hundredths is exactly what a percentage does.

canvas.caption: 30 cells in full rows, 7 in the fourth

screens.prose: Now you do the shading. The slider fills cells in reading order, one hundredth at a time. Its number is the shaded part of the square.
screens.question: Shade 45 of the 100 cells.

hints.text: Four full rows is 40 cells. How many more do you need?

feedback.correct: 45 cells out of 100, and the slider reads 0.45.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count four full rows, then 5 more cells.

byKey.half: You shaded half the square, 50 cells. Take it back by 5 cells.

explain.text: The 45 cells you shaded are $\tfrac{45}{100}$ of the square, and the slider read 0.45. **Per cent** means per hundred, so this is also 45 per cent, written 45%. Three names for one amount.

screens.prose: So a **percentage** is a count of hundredths. The sign % stands for out of 100.
screens.question: What percentage of the square is shaded?

hints.text: How many cells are in one row?
This first cell is 1 out of 100. A full row holds 10 such cells.
Six rows of 10 cells is 60 cells, which is 60 out of 100.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the shaded cells: that count is the percentage.

byKey.rows: You typed 6, the number of rows. Each row is 10 cells, so 6 rows is 60 cells.
byKey.decimal: You typed the decimal 0.6. The box asks for a percentage: 0.6 is 60 hundredths, so type 60.

explain.text: Six rows of 10 make 60 cells, so $\tfrac{60}{100} = 0.6 = 60\%$. Each whole row is 10%, a handy unit for later. You turned a decimal into a percentage by counting its hundredths.

screens.prose: The dashed lines cut the square into four equal quarters. Three of them are shaded.
screens.question: What is $\tfrac{3}{4}$ as a percentage?

hints.text: How many cells are in one quarter?
One quarter is a 5 by 5 block.
One quarter is 25 cells. Three quarters is 75 cells, which is 75 out of 100.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the cells in one quarter, then take three of them.

byKey.digits: You wrote the 3 and the 4 side by side. Count the shaded cells instead: each quarter holds 25.
byKey.decimal: You typed 0.75, the decimal. As a percentage, 0.75 is 75 hundredths, so type 75.

explain.text: Each quarter holds 25 cells, so $\tfrac{3}{4} = \tfrac{3 \times 25}{4 \times 25} = \tfrac{75}{100} = 75\%$. You scaled quarters up to hundredths. Any fraction whose bottom goes into 100 converts this way.

screens.prose: The square becomes a line. It runs from 0 to 1, marked in tenths, and the whole line is 100%.
screens.question: Drag the point to 40%.

hints.text: How many hundredths is 40%?
40 hundredths is the same as 4 tenths. Count four tenth-steps from 0.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. 40% is 40 hundredths of the whole line.

byKey.four-hundredths: You placed 0.04, which is 4%. 40% is 40 hundredths, the same as 4 tenths.

explain.text: 40% is $\tfrac{40}{100}$, which simplifies to $\tfrac{4}{10} = 0.4$. You placed it four tenths along. On a line from 0 to 1, a percentage sits that many hundredths along.

screens.prose: Percentages can pass 100%. A share price that ends at 125% of its start has gone past the whole. This line runs from 0 to 2.
screens.question: Drag the point to 125%.

hints.text: 100% is the whole, at 1. How much further is 25%?
125% is 125 hundredths, which is 1.25. Go to 1, then one more quarter-step.

feedback.correct: 125% is 1.25: one whole and a quarter more.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Turn 125% into hundredths, then into a decimal.

byKey.thousandths: You placed 0.125, as if 125% were 125 thousandths. It is 125 hundredths, which is 1.25.
byKey.capped: You stopped at 100%. A percentage can go past the whole: 125% is a quarter beyond 1.

explain.text: 125% is $\tfrac{125}{100} = 1.25$: one whole and a quarter more. Nothing stops a count of hundredths at 100. A position that has grown by a quarter is worth 125% of its start.

screens.prose: A savings account pays 0.5% interest a year. A spreadsheet needs the rate as a decimal.

state.caption: One cell is 1% of the square

screens.question: What is 0.5% as a decimal?

options.why: You dropped the % sign without dividing by 100. 0.5 is half the square, which is 50%.
You moved the point one place. 0.05 is 5 hundredths, which is 5%: five whole cells.

hints.text: 1% is one cell, $\tfrac{1}{100}$. How big is half of one cell?
This one cell is 1%, which is 0.01. 0.5% is half of it.

feedback.correct: Half of one hundredth is five thousandths: 0.005.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. 0.5% is less than one cell of the square.

byKey.half: You read 0.5% as 0.5. That drops the % sign without dividing by 100, and turns half a cell into half the square.

explain.text: 0.5% is half of one cell, and one cell is 0.01. So $0.5\% = \tfrac{0.5}{100} = 0.005$. Dropping the sign without dividing by 100 makes a rate a hundred times too big.

canvas.caption: 0.5% is half of this one cell

screens.prose: Every time, you moved between three names for one amount. A percentage counts hundredths, so: $$p\% = \frac{p}{100}, \qquad 37\% = \frac{37}{100} = 0.37$$ To go from a percentage to a decimal, divide by 100. To go back, multiply by 100.
screens.question: Write 0.085 as a percentage.

options.why: You read 0.085 as 85 hundredths. The 8 is in the hundredths place, so it is 8.5 hundredths.
You added the sign without multiplying by 100. 0.085% is less than a tenth of one cell.
You moved the point three places. Multiplying by 100 moves it two.

hints.text: Multiply by 100: the point moves two places right.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the decimal by 100 to count its hundredths.

explain.text: 0.085 holds 8.5 hundredths, so it is 8.5%. Multiplying by 100 counts the hundredths. A percentage need not be a whole number.

screens.prose: Eight does not divide 100 into whole pieces, so scaling the bottom to 100 is awkward. Put the lines in order to turn $\tfrac{3}{8}$ into a percentage.
screens.question: Put the lines in order.

lines.text: $\tfrac{3}{8} = 3 \div 8$, because a fraction is a division.
$3 \div 8 = 0.375$, sharing 3 among 8 one place at a time.
$\tfrac{37.5}{100} = 37.5\%$, because per cent means per hundred.

hints.text: Start from the fraction itself, and end with the % sign.
Fraction, then division, then hundredths, then the percentage.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each line must follow from the one above it.

explain.text: Dividing gives a decimal for any fraction. Counting its hundredths then gives the percentage. Three eighths is 37.5 hundredths, so 37.5%.

screens.prose: A dataset stores daily returns as decimals. A return of 0.034 means the price rose by 0.034 of its value. A report must quote each return as a percentage.
screens.question: What should the report show for Tuesday?

hints.text: Multiply the decimal by 100.
Monday shows how: 0.034 became 3.4%.
$-0.008 \times 100 = -0.8$, so the report shows −0.8%.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the decimal by 100 and keep its sign.

byKey.one-place: You moved the point one place, giving −8%. Multiplying by 100 moves it two places: −0.8%.
byKey.decimal: You typed the decimal −0.008 into a percentage box. Multiply by 100 first: type −0.8.
byKey.sign: You dropped the minus sign. Tuesday's price fell, so the return is negative.

explain.text: Moving the point two places turns −0.008 into −0.8%. A fall of 0.8% is under 1%, and it is easy to misquote as 8%. That slip makes a quiet day look like a crash.

ideas: A percentage counts hundredths: 37% is 37 out of 100.
A fraction, a decimal and a percentage can name the same amount.
Percentages can be below 1% or above 100%.

formula.name: Percentage and decimal
formula.note: Divide by 100 for the decimal. Multiply the decimal by 100 for the percentage.

summary.trap: 0.5% is 0.005, not 0.5. Divide by 100 before you drop the % sign.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Scale the bottom up to 100.

byKey.digits: You wrote 7 and 25 side by side. Multiply top and bottom by 4 to reach hundredths.
byKey.flipped: You divided 25 by 7. The fraction means 7 divided by 25.

quiz.prose: A fund charges a fee of 2.5% a year. A spreadsheet needs the fee as a decimal.
quiz.question: What is 2.5% as a decimal?

byKey.one-place: You moved the point one place. 0.25 is 25%. Dividing by 100 moves it two places.
byKey.no-scale: You dropped the % sign without dividing by 100. That makes the fee a hundred times too big.

explain.text: 2.5% is 2.5 hundredths, so $\tfrac{2.5}{100} = 0.025$. The point moves two places left.

options.why: $\tfrac{3}{5}$ is 60 hundredths, 60%. 0.61 is one hundredth more.
You compared 59 with 0.61 without converting. 59% is 59 hundredths, below both 0.61 and $\tfrac{3}{5}$.
You read 0.065 as 65%. It is 6.5 hundredths, so only 6.5%.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write each one as a percentage first.

explain.text: As percentages: $\tfrac{3}{5} = 60\%$, $0.61 = 61\%$, $59\%$ and $0.065 = 6.5\%$. Put on one scale, 61% is largest.

quiz.prose: A share ends the year at 1.2 times its starting price.
quiz.question: What percentage of the starting price is the end price?

widget.label: End price as a percentage of the start

byKey.twelve: You read 1.2 as 12%. 1.2 is 120 hundredths, so 120%.
byKey.rise: You gave the rise, 20%. The question asks for the whole end price as a percentage of the start.

explain.text: $1.2 \times 100 = 120$, so the end price is 120% of the start. That is the whole start price, 100%, plus a rise of 20%.
